variants.name: Explicit loop with state in locals (portable default)
variants.implementation_notes: C++ inherits C's position: no standard guarantee of tail-call elimination, so the portable realization is the loop the pattern describes - parameters become locals or one small state struct, the tail call becomes an assignment plus continue, the base case becomes the guard. GCC and Clang both document sibling/tail-recursive call optimization at -O2 and above, which makes a self-recursive helper free in release builds and expensive in debug builds; wrap the loop in the function that had the accumulator parameter and the public signature stays unchanged.
pitfalls: The same source compiles to constant-stack code under -O2 and to a frame-per-step recursion under -O0 or after an unrelated wrapper is added later; C++ gives no diagnostic either way.
RAII work after the call - a local with a non-trivial destructor, a returned owner, a scope guard - is real work after the tail call and keeps the frame alive.
An indirect call (std::function, a virtual step) may not be eliminated by the sibling-call pass, so performance-critical iterations should stay non-virtual or be rewritten.

variants.name: Standard-library fold replaces the accumulator loop
variants.implementation_notes: When the tail recursion is an accumulation over a range, the accumulation loop already exists in the standard library: std::accumulate(first, last, init) performs exactly the step-and-carry the accumulator parameter encodes, and C++23's std::ranges::fold_left is the range-friendly spelling. The recursion disappears entirely, the stack is constant by construction, and the algorithm states only the combining operation. Use it whenever the iteration is a fold; a state machine with branching transitions still needs the explicit loop.
pitfalls: std::accumulate's default operation is addition: passing a lambda whose return type differs from the accumulator type forces a conversion per step and can change the result type silently.
Folds consume the whole range eagerly; a loop that stops early (break on a condition) corresponds to std::find_if plus an explicit step, not to accumulate.
fold_left is C++23; a C++17 codebase must stay with accumulate or hand-written loops, so the variant floor matters when binding.

variants.name: Tail call enforced with [[clang::musttail]]
variants.implementation_notes: Clang's musttail attribute turns the optimization into a language requirement: the compiler must emit a tail call even with optimizations disabled, and it guarantees the call can be optimized on every supported target. The constraints are checked at compile time - the returned expression must be the call, argument and return types must be compatible, and non-trivial destructors or cleanup after the call make the program invalid. That is the point: it converts the silent de-optimization failure into a build error, which makes it the honest way to rely on elimination in C++. GCC has no equivalent, so the same code needs the loop there.
pitfalls: Cleanup after the call (a local's destructor, an owning return value) makes the program ill-formed under musttail - restructuring into POD state is usually the fix.
Argument and return types must match closely enough for the ABI to forward them; wrappers that take and return different types cannot be tail-called and must be folded into one state struct.
Clang-only: portability demands a fallback loop or an ifdef, so the attribute is best confined to leaf modules.
